item.title: samQEq: universal charge equilibration for molecules and conductors
item.description: arXiv:2611.03687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Charge equilibration assigns atomic charges by equalizing an atomic chemical potential built from electronegativity, hardness and the Coulomb interaction. Under one global constraint it lets charge flow without limit between molecules, which fluctuating-charge models prevent with one neutrality constraint per molecule. A metal needs the opposite: a global constraint and a hardness near zero, and there the charge operator becomes indefinite unless it includes each charge's own self-energy. Here, we present samQEq (solids-and-molecules QEq), a unified charge-equilibration package for LAMMPS that combines the two constructions in one energy functional and one matrix-free solve. An orthogonal projector imposes one neutrality constraint per molecule, and the finite-width self-energy of a Gaussian charge on designated conductor types, narrower than the conductor's own Gaussian, keeps the conductor's part of the operator positive definite at any hardness. On a gold slab carrying a water film, the operator stays definite down to the conductor limit of the model, the metal screens a point charge by a constant amount at every height beyond 4 {\AA}, and the film's charges stay bounded under dynamics. Reciprocal-space electrostatics is evaluated inside the matrix-vector product, and three distinct shielding kernels are run-time settings. We verify the implementation by reproducing a published fluctuating-charge water model without refitting, and the native ReaxFF charge-equilibration step to approximately $10^{-9}\,e$. On a single four-V100 node the largest tested systems run at approximately twice the throughput of a 128-core CPU node. samQEq thus provides one charge-equilibration layer for molecules, conductors and the interfaces between them.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Solan, David Sun, Tod A. Pascal

item.title: SCANO: Restoring Boundary-Condition Completeness in Sampled Meshes with a Sliced-Cross-Attention Neural Operator for 3D Thermal Fields
item.description: arXiv:2611.04603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Training neural operators on million-cell meshes can exceed GPU memory limits. Models are therefore trained on subsamples and deployed on whole meshes or selected regions. However, subsampling can distort boundary information, degrading accuracy. We ask when boundary conditioning under sampling stays consistent with whole-mesh training, and how to aggregate and inject boundary data. Representing the solution as an integral of boundary data against type-dependent measures, we show that subsampling distorts this conditioning in three ways: incomplete boundary coverage or a sample-dependent global state, face weighting by count rather than area, and compression of boundary inputs into a low-dimensional vector. This analysis yields four measurable consistency conditions checkable before training. We satisfy them with two backbone-agnostic modules. Boundary Quadrature Attention (BQA) aggregates all boundary faces, typed and area-weighted, into slice tokens that every query point reads at every layer. Anchored Global State (AGS) estimates the global state from anchors independent of the sampled points. Adding both to a scalable message-passing and slice-attention backbone yields SCANO. We evaluate the approach on controlled and public benchmarks and a data-centre thermal simulation dataset (DCTS) containing million-cell meshes. On both benchmarks, BQA improves every backbone, reducing whole-mesh error up to 15-fold. On all three datasets, AGS aligns regional with whole-mesh predictions, cutting regional error at least tenfold for most backbones on the public benchmark. Together, the modules nearly halve the best original backbone's whole-mesh error on both benchmarks. SCANO predicts a room-scale field in under one second, over 100 times faster than whole-room anchor self-attention.
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Li, Zhiwei Cao, Qingang Zhang, Ruihang Wang, Binyang Song, Yonggang Wen

item.title: On flow unsteadiness in strongly separated high-speed ramp flows using kinetic and data-driven methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.04684v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The gas dynamics of high speed flows over several compression-expansion ramp geometries with large separation regions were investigated using a particle kinetic approach and data driven methods. These large separation regions allow study of the role of scaled angle predicted by triple deck theory on recirculation strength, separation size, and appearance of secondary recirculation regions, all of which lead to flow unsteadiness. Examining four different free stream conditions for the same geometry using the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) approach, we show that the stability of single recirculation in the separation region is more sensitive to wall temperature and free stream velocity than physical ramp angle. Stability in this context refers to appearance of secondary separation regions. In addition, configurations with similar types of recirculation regions from literature considered, we find that general trends regarding unsteadiness, such as appearance of secondary recirculation regions, mostly hold; however, the flows are too complex to be characterized by only scaled angle. Thus, stochastic flowfields generated by DSMC were investigated using data driven methods, namely spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and dynamic mode decomposition. We found that both methods yield similar frequency components and mode shapes for spatio-temporal coherent structures of unsteady DSMC flows. With the help of these structures, the main mechanisms of unsteadiness were identified as oscillations of the reattachment shock, Kelvin-Helmholtz like instability of the shear layer, and c-shaped mode of the separation bubble. This is the first time SPOD has been applied to a DSMC generated flowfield and compared with DMD.
item.dc:creator: Irmak Taylan Karpuzcu, Mert Senkardesler, Deborah A. Levin

item.title: ConvexAD: differentiable phase retrieval with geometric regularization for high-strain, low-signal Bragg coherent diffraction imaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.05020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bragg Coherent Diffraction Imaging (BCDI) relies on phase retrieval (PR), a non-convex, ill-posed inverse problem whose conditioning is degraded by factors like noise, partial coherence, and strain or crystallographic defects in the imaged nanocrystal. Conventional approaches, including alternating projections and deep learning methods, represent the object on a dense voxel grid, which is prone to amplitude-phase mixing and becomes increasingly ill-posed under these factors, often preventing reliable three-dimensional mapping of the particle's shape and strain. Here we present ConvexAD, a gradient descent PR model that parametrizes the object shape as a convex polyhedron, built by the intersection of half-spaces and enforces flat amplitude within it by construction. This geometric regularization eliminates amplitude-phase mixing and reduces the number of trainable parameters, hence facilitating the convergence of the PR. Implemented in JAX for native GPU acceleration and forward-model flexibility, ConvexAD is validated on simulated and experimental BCDI data, where it outperforms conventional and deep learning assisted PR at high strain, low signal, and reduced coherence, extending the conditions under which quantitative BCDI reconstruction is achievable.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Masto, Ewen Bellec, Etienne Polack, Jiangtao Zhao, Vincent Favre-Nicolin, Steven J. Leake, Tobias Sch\"ulli, Marie-Ingrid Richard

item.title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.05327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work presents an optimization-based remap approach for arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics that preserves sharp features and physical bounds while conserving global quantities such as volume, mass, momentum, and total energy. Achieving these properties is the main challenge in remap methods. The presented approach is well-suited for high-order finite element (FE) discretizations and ALE methods that allow for large, purely Lagrangian displacements between successive remeshing and remapping steps. Recent advances in parallel, GPU-capable interpolation routines enable the initial transfer of all fields via direct physical-space interpolation, avoiding computationally costly and diffusive pseudo-transient PDE-based advection. The interpolation produces bounded fields with minimal numerical diffusion. However, it may violate the desired conservation of global properties. Thus, a subsequent optimization step restores conservation while preserving physical bounds. The presented method provides minimally diffusive remapping of finite element fields of arbitrary order. Moreover, it directly remaps quantities defined at integration points, eliminating the need for projection onto finite element spaces. The approach also mitigates typical challenges associated with synchronizing primal variables and conserved quantities in advection-based remap methods. The proposed optimization-based remap method is evaluated using standard two- and three-dimensional remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Keith, Dohyun Kim, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Cosmin G. Petra, Mathias R. Schmidt, Vladimir Z. Tomov

item.title: Advanced computational methods for simulating the classical hydrogen atom in stochastic electrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.22393v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic electrodynamics (SED) is a theory of nature seeking to derive key aspects of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics from a purely classical physics perspective. While SED has been successful in many areas, it has had mixed success when addressing the classical hydrogen atom bathed in classical electromagnetic zero-point radiation. Because analytical approaches are largely intractable, advanced numerical simulation methods are required. To address this, we develop a pseudo-wave formulation that integrates the solid angle in k-space utilizing symmetry, resulting in a significantly reduced memory footprint and lower computational overhead for generating the zero-point radiation spectrum. This optimization is paired with a logarithmic frequency grid, a sliding window tracking the instantaneous Keplerian frequency, and a Tukey smoothing function to eliminate discrete force discontinuities. Integrated via an adaptive RK4 algorithm with step-doubling across highly dense grids of up to 100-million bins, these techniques demonstrate the asymptotic convergence of ensemble stability. We show that increasing grid resolution in the high-frequency domain systematically mitigates artificial electron decay, yielding a simulated probability density function that closely aligns with the quantum mechanical ground state P(r). Crucially, the simulations exhibit stable, low-eccentricity orbits without any observed atomic ionization events.
item.dc:creator: Daniel C. Cole

item.title: Forecasting Low-Dimensional Navier-Stokes equations via Multi-Dimensional Hybrid Quantum Reservoir Computing
item.description: arXiv:2509.04006v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The prediction of complex dynamics remains an open problem across many domains of physics, where nonlinearities and multiscale interactions severely limit the reliability of conventional forecasting methods. Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for information processing by exploiting the high dimensionality of the Hilbert space, where the dynamics of quantum systems take place. Here, we introduce a hybrid quantum-classical reservoir architecture capable of handling multivariate time series through quantum evolution combined with classical memory enhancement. Our model employs a five-qubit transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian with input-modulated dynamics and temporal multiplexing, enabling the encoding of input signals over multiple timescales. We apply this framework to two paradigmatic models of chaotic behavior in fluid dynamics, where multiscale dynamics and nonlinearities play a dominant role: a low-dimensional truncation of the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations and the Lorenz-63 system. By systematically scanning the quantum system's parameter space, we identify regions that maximize forecasting performance, as measured by the Valid Prediction Time. The observed robustness and reliable performances for both dynamical systems suggest that this hybrid quantum approach offers a flexible platform for modelling complex nonlinear time series.
item.dc:creator: L. Salatino, L. Mariani, A. Giordano, F. D'Amore, C. Mastroianni, L. Pontieri, A. Vinci, C. Gencarelli, L. Primavera, F. Plastina, J. Settino, F. Carbone

item.title: Loss of altermagnetic order and smooth restoration of Kramers' spin degeneracy with increasing temperature in CrSb and MnTe
item.description: arXiv:2603.15035v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We describe how thermally induced spin fluctuations modify the electronic structures of two prototypical altermagnets, CrSb and MnTe, via application of the disordered local moment picture. For both materials, our self-consistent, ab initio calculations demonstrate that local magnetic moments persist on Cr and Mn atoms in their paramagnetic states, necessitating a spin-polarised description of the electronic structure even above the N\'eel temperature, $T_\mathrm{N}$. Moreover, Kramers' spin degeneracy, which is broken for both materials in their altermagnetic ground states, is shown to be smoothly restored - on the average - as the local moments thermally disorder. In metallic CrSb, this occurs at temperatures well below $T_\mathrm{N}$ and the signature effects of its altermagnetism are lost as the magnetic disorder induces heavy smearing of strongly dispersive electronic states around the Fermi energy. By contrast, in semiconducting MnTe, with its band gap largely unaffected by magnetic disorder, the spin degeneracy only returns at temperatures close to and above $T_\mathrm{N}$. We quantify the temperature dependence of the altermagnetic order parameter and the underlying electronic structures of both materials, with implications for their spin transport and spectroscopic properties.
item.dc:creator: Christopher D. Woodgate, Nabil Menai, Arthur Ernst, Julie B. Staunton

item.title: An efficient finite element formulation for Newtonian noise analysis
item.description: arXiv:2603.15157v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Einstein Telescope is a third-generation underground gravitational wave observatory designed to achieve an unprecedented sensitivity down to 3 Hz. Waves propagating in the soil due to anthropogenic or natural vibration sources generate density fluctuations which cause gravitational attraction, resulting in motion of the mirrors of the laser interferometer known as Newtonian noise. A finite element formulation is presented, which evaluates the total Newtonian noise, as well as the bulk and surface contributions, from a seismic wave field defined on a finite element mesh, using Gaussian quadrature. Linear and quadratic tetrahedral (4-node and 10-node) and brick (8-node and 20-node) finite elements are supported. The corresponding volume and surface integrals are expressed in terms of finite element coupling matrices that depend only on the geometry and material properties. The formulation is verified for plane P- and S-waves propagating in an elastic homogeneous full space with a mirror suspended in a spherical cavity, assuming that the wavelength is much larger than the radius of the cavity, so that wave scattering can be ignored. Excellent agreement with analytical solutions is obtained. Similar good agreement is reported for the Newtonian noise on a test mass suspended at a finite distance above the free surface of a homogeneous elastic halfspace in which a Rayleigh wave propagates. The methodology has been implemented in the ANNA Newtonian Noise Analysis toolbox which runs in the MATLAB programming and numeric computing platform and is compatible with the open-source GNU Octave Scientific Programming Language; a Python version is also available. The proposed finite element framework provides a physically consistent and computationally efficient approach for computing gravitational-seismic coupling in heterogeneous media.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: P. Reumers, X. Kuci, S. Fran\c{c}ois and G. Degrande. An efficient finite element formulation for Newtonian noise analysis. Computer Physics Communications, 329, 110390, 2026
item.dc:creator: Pieter Reumers, Xhorxha Kuci, Stijn Fran\c{c}ois, Geert Degrande

item.title: Resource-efficient energy-based operator selection in fermionic ADAPT-VQE via exact Hamiltonian transformation
item.description: arXiv:2606.04786v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Energy-based variants of ADAPT-VQE select operators by minimizing a one-parameter cost function for each candidate generator. In fermionic implementations, the cost of reconstructing this function often becomes a bottleneck. We reduce this cost using exact fermionic Hamiltonian transformations to obtain a generator-dependent partition of the Hamiltonian that reconstruct the same one-parameter energy function from fragment measurements. This method reproduces the fermionic Rotoselect scoring function exactly with approximately half the Pauli-string measurements. We use this formulation to benchmark the gradient-based and energy-based selection approaches in combination with two ansatz-optimization strategies---$\textit{last}$, where only the appended operator is optimized, and $\textit{full}$, where the full ansatz is re-optimized---and with both fixed-orbital and orbital-optimized formulations. The benchmark comprises $\text{LiH}$, $\text{BeH}_2$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at both equilibrium and stretched geometries. In the most weakly correlated system, pairing energy-based selection with $\textit{last}$ optimization enables the resource-efficient construction of an accurate ansatz, which avoids any VQE optimization. As correlation increases, full ansatz re-optimization and orbital optimization become the main factors governing convergence and overall resource cost. This study shows how exact Hamiltonian transformations provide an effective route to reducing the measurement overhead of fermionic energy-based ADAPT-VQE. Moreover, the benchmark clarifies the relative role of operator selection approach, parameter reoptimization strategy, and orbital optimization in the performance of ADAPT-VQE.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Rossi, Erik Rosendahl Kjellgren, Artur F. Izmaylov, Stephan P. A. Sauer, Karl Michael Ziems, Sonia Coriani

item.title: Sparse stochastic digital twins can outperform exact ones
item.description: arXiv:2606.16219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Digital twins are often built under the assumption that greater model fidelity leads to better downstream performance. We show that this is not always the case: retaining weakly dependent or auxiliary degrees of freedom can increase the dimensionality of learning and control problems enough that a sparse stochastic surrogate outperforms even an exact high-dimensional model. To identify such structure, we introduce a framework for dependence discovery directly at the level of the full conditional law. The method combines conditional generative modeling with Gaussian-process distillation and kernel mode decomposition to quantify how strongly individual variables enter the conditional distribution, including through variability, tails, multimodality, and other features invisible to the conditional mean. The resulting dependence structure can be used both to construct sparse stochastic digital twins from data and to reduce known high-dimensional models for downstream tasks. In a modified Lunar Lander problem, an eight-dimensional sparse surrogate yields better control performance than the exact 109-dimensional simulator despite lower transition fidelity. A stochastic heat-equation example shows that the framework recovers sparse structure in a 102-dimensional data-driven setting and produces a more effective surrogate than one conditioned on all candidate inputs, while economic data demonstrate its use for identifying time-varying memory structure. These results show that model fidelity and downstream utility are distinct objectives, and that dependence discovery provides a practical route to sparse stochastic digital twins.
item.dc:creator: Zongren Zou, Th\'eo Bourdais, Ricardo Baptista, Houman Owhadi

item.title: Chemical potentials from structure factors: I. Neutral multi-component mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2608.08357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The chemical potentials of multi-component mixtures underlie many physical and chemical phenomena, but remain challenging to compute. The S0 method enables the computation of chemical potentials from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, by leveraging the thermodynamic relationship between particle number fluctuations and derivatives of chemical potentials, followed by numerical integration along different compositions. Here we generalize the S0 method from two-component mixtures to neutral multi-component mixtures. We first extend the statistical mechanical formalism to high-dimensional compositional space, and then introduce a Gaussian process integration scheme combined with active learning to efficiently integrate chemical potentials and sample diverse compositions. We use this method to compute the mixing free energies of a molten metal alloy, and the solubilities of two paracetamol polymorphs in water-ethanol solvents. The extended S0 method provides a practical and scalable route for computing chemical potentials in neutral bulk multi-component mixtures from atomistic simulations.
item.dc:creator: Roya Savoj, Xiaoyu Wang, Musahid Ahmed, Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Chemical potentials from structure factors: II. Charged multi-component mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2608.30060v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The chemical potentials of charged multi-component mixtures are central to electrolyte thermodynamics, but remain difficult to compute from atomistic simulations. The S0 method enables computing chemical potentials of mixtures from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. Here we extend the S0 method to charged mixtures by combining the composition-space framework developed in Part I: Neutral Multi-component Mixtures with a Coulombic treatment of the small-wavenumber limits of static structure factors. This approach separates thermodynamically relevant neutral composition fluctuations from forbidden macroscopic charge fluctuations, and further accounts for charge-neutrality constraints. We use the method to compute the chemical potentials of multiple-halide aqueous salt solutions, elucidating the ion-specific thermodynamic effects. We also calculate the mixing free energies of molten salt mixtures, demonstrating the importance of correctly describing long-wavelength electrostatic correlations.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Wang, Roya Savoj, Musahid Ahmed, Bingqing Cheng

item.title: A Square-Root Barrier to Quantum Gate Speed under Linear Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2609.19280v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Faster quantum gates can reduce the decoherence accumulated during a computation, but in superconducting processors, speeding up gates often involves stronger microwave pulses, which can increase leakage, off-resonant excitation, stray-field errors, and crosstalk. This creates a central energy--speed--error tradeoff: can quantum state engineering make a gate faster without paying proportionally more drive energy? We address this question by treating the driving pulse as a quantum bosonic field rather than a classical waveform. For a finite-dimensional system coupled linearly to that field, we prove that gate transition rates at fixed trace distance between the initial and final system states grow at most as the square root of the pulse energy, under pulse-uniformity conditions, without assuming an upper bound on the coupling strength. The bound permits arbitrary pulse states, including squeezed and non-Gaussian states, as well as drive--system entanglement and back action; coherent Gaussian pulses attain its energy exponent. Thus squeezing or other state engineering alone cannot replace the square-root energy law of a conventional linear drive by the linear scaling allowed by general quantum speed limits. Achieving that improvement requires changing the interaction class, in addition to using a suitable nonclassical pulse, thereby identifying interaction nonlinearity as an essential resource for relaxing the practical gate-speed error tradeoff.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Restrepo Gaviria, Mischa P. Woods
